definition: Inherent risk is the risk as it stands before any controls are applied. Residual risk is what remains after controls are in place; it is then accepted, transferred or reduced further.
example: A public web server faces high inherent risk of compromise; after a WAF, patching and MFA for admins, the leftover chance of a zero-day attack is the residual risk the owner signs off on.
keyPoints: Inherent = no controls; residual = after controls
Risk is never zero, so some residual risk always remains
Residual risk should fall within the risk appetite, or more controls are needed
Accepting residual risk is a decision recorded by the risk owner
Controls that only move risk elsewhere (insurance) transfer it rather than remove it

definition: The average time a part that cannot be repaired runs before it fails and has to be replaced.
example: A data center runs 1,000 SSDs rated at an MTTF of 1.5 million hours. On average that is about one failed drive every 1,500 hours (roughly two months), so the team keeps spare drives on hand.
keyPoints: MTTF: parts that are replaced, not repaired
MTBF: repairable systems, time between one failure and the next
MTTR: average time to repair
Higher MTTF means more reliable
A fleet average, not a promise for one part: 1.5 million hours does not mean one drive lasts 171 years
Used to swap parts out before they are expected to fail, ideally from figures for your own environment

definition: A person who oversees an organization's compliance with data protection law, advises on it and is the contact for regulators and data subjects. The GDPR requires one for public bodies and for organizations whose core work involves large-scale monitoring of people or large-scale processing of sensitive or criminal conviction data. CompTIA's acronym list calls the role data privacy officer.
example: An online advertising firm that tracks millions of users' behavior appoints a DPO who reports to the board and reviews every new tracking project for GDPR compliance.
keyPoints: Required under GDPR Article 37 for public bodies (courts acting as courts excepted), large-scale systematic monitoring, or large-scale special category or criminal conviction data
Reports to the highest level of management
Must not be told how to do the job or be penalized for doing it
May hold other duties only if they create no conflict of interest
Advises and monitors; the controller stays responsible for compliance

term: SOC reports (SOC 1, SOC 2, SOC 3; Type I vs Type II)
definition: Independent auditor reports on a service organization's controls. SOC 1 covers controls that affect customers' financial reporting; SOC 2 covers one or more trust services categories (security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy); SOC 3 covers the same ground as SOC 2 in a shorter form anyone may read. A Type I report judges control design at one date; a Type II also tests whether the controls worked over a period.
example: Before signing with a cloud backup vendor, a company asks for its SOC 2 Type II report, which shows the auditor tested the vendor's access controls over the past twelve months.
keyPoints: SOC 1: financial reporting controls, for customers and their auditors
SOC 2: the trust services criteria, shared only with specific readers such as customers
SOC 3: general use, no detailed test results, can be posted publicly
Type I: designed well as of a date; Type II: designed well and operating effectively over a period
Type II gives more assurance; it is what most customers ask for
